item.title: Pop!_OS 26.04 LTS fixes the biggest problem with making your desktop look good on COSMIC
item.itunes:title: Pop!_OS 26.04 LTS fixes the biggest problem with making your desktop look good on COSMIC
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Summary

  • Pop!_OS 26.04 LTS adds Constellations — quick theme-like visual styles for COSMIC.
  • Switch Constellations via Settings > Desktop > Appearance; no more DWM digging.
  • Grab Pop!_OS 26.04 to try Constellations now, or wait for it to arrive on other distros later.

The first half of building your home on Linux is finding the distro that resonates with you; the second half is making everything look good. Because Linux has some really amazing customization options, you may find yourself wanting to change things up every so often.

For a while, changing how your PC looks on the COSMIC desktop environment was a bit of a chore. However, the newest version of its home distro, Pop!_OS 26.04 LTS, has added a way to change how your desktop looks with ease, and it even has a fitting name.

Pop!_OS 26.04 LTS introduces Constellations to COSMIC

Much like the real thing, these Constellations bring lots of individual parts together

Over on the System76 blog (via OMGUbuntu), the team has announced Constellations within the COSMIC DE. They act like themes, allowing you to go between different visual styles on the fly. They're also positioned in a far friendlier place within the OS than the current options; instead of digging through your settings for the Desktop Window Management panel, you just need to visit Settings > Desktop > Appearance, and you're good to go.

If you want to give Constellations a spin right now, head over to the System76 Pop!_OS download page to get the newest version of COSMIC. If you'd rather use a different distro, there's a good chance that you can add COSMIC to it as a desktop environment. It may not be fully up-to-date right now, but Constellations should still arrive in a future update later on.

I switched to the COSMIC Linux desktop, and I can't wait for the future

COSMIC is out of this world, even with its flaws

15
By  João Carrasqueira

item.title: This TP-Link 1Gbps USB-C to Ethernet Adapter is under $10 now
item.itunes:title: This TP-Link 1Gbps USB-C to Ethernet Adapter is under $10 now
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Wi-Fi works fine until a game download crawls or an online match drops at the wrong moment. Plugging in a cable is the usual way around that, and a USB-to-Ethernet adapter lets you do it on a Nintendo Switch. The TP-Link USB-to-Ethernet adapter is $9.29 on Amazon for Black Friday, down from its $16.99 list price. It's listed as a 1Gbps adapter that supports the Switch.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover
TP-Link USB to Ethernet Adapter
Brand
TP-Link
USB Version
USB-C 3.0

The TP-Link UE306 is a foldable USB 3.0 to Gigabit Ethernet adapter that adds a wired RJ45 port to laptops and the Nintendo Switch dock. It supports speeds up to 1000 Mbps, weighs 20 g (0.71 oz), and is plug-and-play on Windows 10/8.1, Linux, and Nintendo Switch.

See at Amazon

A simple fix for unstable internet

Wired internet for your Switch

You get one USB 3.0 input and one RJ45 Ethernet port. Plug the adapter into a USB port, run an Ethernet cable to your router, and you've got a wired connection in place of Wi-Fi. That matters on a console in particular, since online play and big game updates both depend on a steady connection. Your actual speeds will still depend on your internet plan.

Setup is simple. TP-Link says the adapter is plug-and-play on the Nintendo Switch, Windows 10, Windows 8.1, and Linux, so you shouldn't need to install anything on those. Windows 11 is on the supported list, as are Windows 7 and 8, though the latter two require drivers from the TP-Link website.

It's small, too. TP-Link lists it at 2.8 x 1.0 x 0.6 inches (71 x 26 x 16.2mm), and that makes it easy to slip into a bag. At 20g, it won't add much weight to a travel kit. An LED indicator shows network status, and TP-Link lists an AX88179 chipset along with CE and FCC certifications.

Because it works with Windows and Linux, as well as the Nintendo Switch, a single adapter can connect your console to a computer.

It isn't for everyone. If your Wi-Fi already holds up well, you won't gain much, and you'll need your own Ethernet cable if you pick this up. But if your Switch sits far from the router, or you have a laptop or desktop without an Ethernet port, a cable is a simple fix. The dollar discount is small, at $7 off the $16.99 listed price, but at under $10 the risk is low too.

At $9.29 on Amazon, it's an easy one to pick up if Wi-Fi has been getting in the way of your Switch. The listing is sold by Amazon itself. We don't have an end date for the Black Friday sale, so it's hard to say how long the price will last. Grab the TP-Link USB-to-Ethernet Adapter soon while it's still on sale.

item.title: I ran one Windows command and it showed me every Wi-Fi password I've used since 2019
item.itunes:title: I ran one Windows command and it showed me every Wi-Fi password I've used since 2019
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I've used the same Windows PC for years, so I assumed there wasn't much left for it to surprise me with. Turns out I was wrong, because while poking around some of Windows' older networking tools, I stumbled across something that made me wonder just how much digital baggage I'd been carrying around without even realizing it.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

Finding out that Windows has a surprisingly long memory when it comes to the Wi-Fi networks I've connected to was not on my 2026 bingo card, and here we are. In fact, I was caught off guard by just how much information was still attached to some of those forgotten connections.

5 Windows networking features you should consider using

Windows has a ton of advanced networking features that can make your life easier

1
By  Joe Rice-Jones

Windows remembered Wi-Fi networks I had completely forgotten about

My PC apparently has a better memory than I do

The first thing I did was open Command Prompt and run netsh wlan show profiles. I expected to see the Wi-Fi networks I currently use, perhaps a couple of old ones I'd forgotten to remove. Instead, Windows served up what looked like a small archaeological record of everywhere I'd connected to.

That list included networks I hadn't touched in years. I saw old apartments, workplaces, hotels, family homes, and random connections I couldn't even remember, and they were all sitting there as saved WLAN profiles, even though I had no reason to keep them. Windows had been keeping track of them long after they had stopped being relevant to me.

On second thought, though, I realized that this actually makes sense. Windows saves wireless profiles so it can remember things like the network's configuration and automatically reconnect when you return. The problem, however, is that there's a difference between "I connected to this once," and "I still need Windows to remember this."

The command itself is also refreshingly straightforward. netsh wlan show profiles doesn't reveal passwords or perform any hacking wizardry, though. All it does is ask Windows to list the wireless profiles currently stored on the machine. You can then identify individual profiles by their exact names.

However, all you need to do is add one more argument to the string, and you'll see every Wi-Fi password you've used with those profiles.

My Windows install is ten years old, and a handful of maintenance habits are why it still runs like new

Essential maintenance keeps my old Windows 11 system running smoothly.

21
By  Brian Burgess

One command later, Windows handed me the password

The password was sitting there the entire time

The second command is where things get considerably more interesting. Once I had a profile name, I ran netsh wlan show profile name="NETWORK-NAME" key=clear. Immediately, Windows returned the selected profile's stored configuration, including its security settings that had the Wi-Fi password in plain text under Key Content, "for all to see."

In a nutshell, netsh wlan show profiles gives you the names, and adding the profile name plus key=clear asks Windows to display the stored security information for that specific connection. As you might expect, replacing the network name with another saved profile will let you check that one, too.

Now, this only works with credentials that Windows has actually retained in the saved profile, and what gets returned depends on the network's authentication method and your permissions on the machine. If the profile is gone, there's nothing for netsh to retrieve in the first place.

Still, seeing an old password appear after I had completely forgotten the network existed was bizarre. Windows had simply been keeping the information around quietly, waiting for me to ask for it. Naturally, this made me wonder if I should really be leaving all those old profiles there on my PC.

These 5 home networking tools are essential for any Windows user

Troubleshoot, optimize, and secure your home network like a pro

1
By  Pranav Bhardwaj

The passwords live in XML files on the PC

Thankfully, a PC's secrets don't travel well

Curiosity got the better of me, so I went digging deeper than the netsh output. Windows stores each wireless profile as an XML file on the C drive. Heading to C:\ProgramData\Microsoft\Wlansvc\Profiles\Interfaces showed me the profiles, all organized according to the wireless adapter they belong to.

Opening one of those files doesn't reveal a convenient little password line, though. Instead, the credential that I could see from the command line was represented by an encrypted blob inside the keyMaterial field.

I even tested this by copying one of the profile files to another PC and trying to make sense of it there. As it turned out, nothing happened. The profile wasn't portable, and the netsh command couldn't even conjure up the network adapter, let alone the password from the copied file. Whatever Windows had stored in that blob wasn't useful outside its original environment.

Windows stores the profile's key material in protected form, rather than as a readable password. That means copying the XML file alone doesn't make the password readable; access to the protected key material depends on Windows and the required permissions.

It's not completely bulletproof, though. Someone with access to your PC and sufficient permissions may be able to retrieve a stored Wi-Fi key using Windows tools. That risk is different from simply copying the profile XML file, which contains protected key material rather than a readable password.

What is a public or private network in Windows, and why does it matter?

Choosing the right settings is important

By  João Carrasqueira

Windows isn't leaking your passwords

But you probably don't need all those profiles anymore

Truth be told, this isn't another "Windows is secretly stealing your data" story. This isn't a security flaw with your PC, either. Windows needs to retain Wi-Fi credentials if you expect it to reconnect to networks automatically, and the netsh command just exposes information that your account is already authorized to access. The surprising part is really how long some of these profiles can stick around.

Regardless, I still don't want years of forgotten networks cluttering up my PC, though. Running the show profiles command is a surprisingly good way to see what Windows still remembers, and removing an obsolete profile is just as easy with netsh wlan delete profile name="NETWORK NAME" to remove a particular Wi-Fi network's security data. If you haven't used a network in years, there's little reason to keep its profile around.

The bigger lesson is that Windows has an absurd memory for things most of us consider disposable. I had forgotten half the networks in that list existed, while Windows had dutifully kept their profiles tucked away. It isn't sinister, and it isn't particularly new. It's just another example of Windows quietly remembering far more about your computing history than you probably realized.

13
By  Abhishek Kumar Mishra

Windows has a memory problem, and honestly, so do I

We spend so much time installing utilities to expose information Windows already knows that finding one of these buried tools feels like uncovering a secret passage in your own house. It also makes me wonder how many other perfectly useful commands I've ignored simply because they look like something from Windows XP.

Every now and then, you pull at one seemingly insignificant thread inside Windows and discover an entire layer of functionality underneath it. The netsh command isn't glamorous or new, but it certainly has become a command I'll never forget.

In a nutshell, netsh wlan show profiles gives you the names, and adding the profile name plus key=clear asks Windows to display the stored security information for that specific connection. As you might expect, replacing the network name with another saved profile will let you check that one, too.

Now, this only works with credentials that Windows has actually retained in the saved profile, and what gets returned depends on the network's authentication method and your permissions on the machine. If the profile is gone, there's nothing for netsh to retrieve in the first place.

Still, seeing an old password appear after I had completely forgotten the network existed was bizarre. Windows had simply been keeping the information around quietly, waiting for me to ask for it. Naturally, this made me wonder if I should really be leaving all those old profiles there on my PC.

By  Pranav Bhardwaj

The passwords live in XML files on the PC

Thankfully, a PC's secrets don't travel well

Curiosity got the better of me, so I went digging deeper than the netsh output. Windows stores each wireless profile as an XML file on the C drive. Heading to C:\ProgramData\Microsoft\Wlansvc\Profiles\Interfaces showed me the profiles, all organized according to the wireless adapter they belong to.

Opening one of those files doesn't reveal a convenient little password line, though. Instead, the credential that I could see from the command line was represented by an encrypted blob inside the keyMaterial field.

I even tested this by copying one of the profile files to another PC and trying to make sense of it there. As it turned out, nothing happened. The profile wasn't portable, and the netsh command couldn't even conjure up the network adapter, let alone the password from the copied file. Whatever Windows had stored in that blob wasn't useful outside its original environment.

Windows stores the profile's key material in protected form, rather than as a readable password. That means copying the XML file alone doesn't make the password readable; access to the protected key material depends on Windows and the required permissions.

It's not completely bulletproof, though. Someone with access to your PC and sufficient permissions may be able to retrieve a stored Wi-Fi key using Windows tools. That risk is different from simply copying the profile XML file, which contains protected key material rather than a readable password.

Windows isn't leaking your passwords

But you probably don't need all those profiles anymore

Truth be told, this isn't another "Windows is secretly stealing your data" story. This isn't a security flaw with your PC, either. The surprising part is really how long some of these profiles can stick around.

I had forgotten half the networks in that list existed, while Windows had dutifully kept their profiles tucked away. It isn't sinister, and it isn't particularly new. item.itunes:summary:
My smartphone is supposed to make my life easier, but sometimes it does the exact opposite. Whether I am concentrating on an important project, winding down for the night, or driving, notifications, calls, and random alerts always seem to arrive at the worst possible moment.

Sure, I could manually enable DND or silence my phone every few hours, but that defeats the purpose of owning a smart device. That’s when I decided to explore Samsung’s Routines on my Galaxy S25 Ultra. The results have been effective, and I wish I had set them up much earlier.

My phone stays quiet while I work

My work hours are distraction-free

The last thing I want while writing an article or researching a new topic is a constant stream of notifications from WhatsApp groups, Instagram, and shopping platforms. Instead of manually silencing my Galaxy phone every morning, I set up a dedicated work routine in Samsung’s Routines that automatically kicks in at 10am and ends at 7pm.

When it activates, my phone enables Do Not Disturb, blocks notifications from distracting apps, and only allows calls from important contacts. This way, I don’t have to worry about missing an urgent call from a family member while keeping unnecessary distractions at bay.

I took it a step further by setting a different home screen wallpaper for work hours. It gives me a subtle visual clue that it’s time to focus.

I also have my phone show upcoming calendar events so I can quickly glance at my schedule without opening another app.

The best part is that everything returned to normal at 7pm without any intervention from my end. It’s almost like having two different personalities on the same smartphone. My Galaxy is a productivity-focused device during work hours and switches back to a regular smartphone when I am done for the day.

I turned off one Samsung feature and gained hours of battery life

My Samsung suddenly lasted much longer.

3
By  Parth Shah

My phone knows when I am driving

Android Auto triggers my driving makeover

Considering how frequently I use Android Auto, creating a dedicated driving routine was a no-brainer. When my Galaxy connects to my car’s infotainment system and activates Android Auto, it automatically changes several settings without requiring any input from me.

First, it disables the Always On Display. Since I rely on my car’s infotainment screen for navigation, music playback, and incoming calls, there is little reason for my phone’s display to remain active. My routine also enables Power Saving mode to limit unnecessary background activity and conserve battery during longer journeys.

Another important action is disabling fast charging. Between wireless Android Auto, GPS navigation, mobile data, and music streaming, my Galaxy already has plenty going on in the background. When I plug it into a charger during a journey, disabling fast charging helps reduce additional heat buildup, especially on hot summer afternoons.

What I appreciate most is how seamlessly everything works. Once I reach my destination and disconnect from Android Auto, my Galaxy automatically reverts all these changes. Power saving mode turns off, fast charging returns, and AOD goes back to its previous state. I don’t have to dig through the Settings menu or remember which options I changed before starting my journey.

My phone stops disturbing my sleep

Sunset brings out Android’s quieter side

Unlike my work routine, which follows a fixed schedule, I wanted my nighttime routine to adapt to changing daylight hours throughout the year. Instead of specifying a particular time, I configured my Galaxy to automatically activate the routine at sunset and disable it at sunrise.

As soon as the sun goes down, my phone switches to the dark theme, enables Eye Comfort Shield, and lowers the system and notification volumes.

The warmer display tones and darker interface make browsing websites, reading articles, and catching up on messages more comfortable in a dimly lit room. I also configured the routine to reduce screen brightness and disable unnecessary vibrations so that my phone feels less intrusive during the evening.

It’s a much better approach than manually enabling these settings every night. Since the routine follows local sunrise and sunset times, I don’t have to adjust its schedule as the seasons change. When the sun rises, my Galaxy automatically restores its previous appearance, volume levels, and display settings. There are no reminders to dismiss or toggles to fiddle with.

My phone now knows when to stay quiet

What I love about Samsung’s Routines is that it doesn’t require an elaborate setup to make a major difference. With just three simple rules, my Galaxy knows when I need to concentrate, when I am behind the wheel, and when it’s time to wind down.

If you own a Galaxy phone, I highly recommend exploring Routines before downloading another productivity app or an automation tool.

There just really isn't much new this year.

item.title: Decompilation projects have quietly brought more classic games to PC than any official remaster program
item.itunes:title: Decompilation projects have quietly brought more classic games to PC than any official remaster program
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
When I loaded up Ship of Harkinian for the first time earlier this year, the feeling I got could only be compared to the first time I fired up my Nintendo 64 over 2 decades ago. Emulation is fantastic, but playing a native PC port of one of my favorite games of all time was truly mind-blowing. And the fact that Nintendo wasn't involved anywhere in the development made it even crazier, but decompilation projects like SoH have been spawning in at what seems like an impossible rate.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

Thanks to the persistence of some very dedicated fans, decompilations for classic Nintendo games like Super Mario 64, Majora's Mask, Banjo-Kazooie, Twilight Princess, and many more have brought remaster-like experiences to the PC, and AI has only accelerated this process for other titles. For console exclusives that were simply never going to make it to the PC, these decompilation efforts have done an incredible amount for game preservation — far more than Nintendo or any other publisher has ever done for their own IPs.

Fans have built the library that publishers haven't bothered with

PC ports were never in the cards for these games

Almost all of these PC ports follow one of two approaches. Decompilation is historically the slowest, and it's where developers take a game's machine code and translate it back into human-readable C code, function by function, until it compiles into a byte-for-byte match with the original. Once that exists, a port to Windows, macOS, or Linux becomes a normal programming project rather than a reverse engineering one.

Static recompilation is the other approach, and it uses tools like N64: Recompiled to translate the game's compiled code directly into a PC program your computer can run, without needing a full decompilation. With either approach, a user would have to supply their own copy of the game, and that's the legal loophole these projects are leaning on heavily right now.

While Nintendo has re-released Ocarina of Time for the 3DS and remade it for the Switch 2, the other games I mentioned, like Majora's Mask, Banjo Kazooie, and others, haven't received much of an update besides maybe being made available through Nintendo Online or a 3DS remake. It's not just Nintendo either: Konami's original Silent Hill for the PlayStation hasn't got any kind of true remaster, and on the Xbox side of things, games like Sonic Unleashed were ignored for years before it eventually got a full PC port thanks to fans of the game.

Even for many Xbox titles, PC ports are usually completely off the table for these console exclusives, but the demand would be much lower if publishers offered more ways to experience the game on modern hardware. It can certainly go badly if neglected after the fact (anyone remember Half-Life: Source?), but it's still better than ignoring the classics that made these IPs so popular in the first place.

Emulators save games that publishers have abandoned, but the industry still treats them like piracy

Game preservation often skirts the line between the legal and illegal

By  Tanveer Singh

Static recompilations turned a trickle into a flood

The approach a publisher wouldn't take

Credit: Nintendo / Dusk

A full decompilation is truly painstaking work if done manually — Super Smash Bros. Melee's decompilation efforts took more than six years to complete, and it only gets more complex as the games do. The static recompilation approach was the first big breakthrough behind the flood of PC ports.

When Wiseguy released N64: Recompiled in 2024, its first showcase was a Majora's Mask port that came together in a couple of days, aided by earlier reverse-engineering work. The same toolchain has since produced ports of Star Fox 64, Mario Kart 64, and Banjo-Kazooie, and the Majora's Mask port has picked up more than 120 community mods.

XenonRecomp did the same for an Xbox 360 game with Sonic Unleashed, and PS2Recomp is attempting it for the PlayStation 2. Each new tool turns an entire console library into potential ports. It does a lot of the hard parts for the developers making these PC ports.

Nintendo and other publishers don't take kindly to these recomps

They might be on borrowed time

Publishers do have a fair argument against fans making these recompilations. The IP belongs to them, and any official release using that IP can include things like licensed music or other copyrights that fan projects skim over. The "bring your own copy" principle has kept them safe from being guilty of redistributing game assets, but the truth is, plenty of players don't own the originals, and will find a way to get the files some other way.

Nintendo is infamous for taking legal action against even the smallest of transgressions against their IP. They've pulled down countless videos, websites, and GitHub repos for emulators and recompilation projects, and they're not alone. Other publishers are taking notice, and I think it's only a matter of time before the next shoe drops on these fan projects, even if they have the green light in the eyes of the law right now.

Your old Nintendo 64 games are finally getting unofficial PC ports, and they run better than emulators

Retro titles are getting even better, and it's all thanks to decompilation.

3
By  Adam Conway

The cat is out of the bag

AI has super-charged development of these projects

AI coding agents have made the arduous task of decompilation into more of a waiting game, and that's the second big reason why serious progress on these projects has been made in such a short span of time. The aforementioned Melee decompilation is one excellent example: it was less than half done in November 2025 and reached 100 percent the following September, and the contributor who announced it credited AI assistance in getting things across the finish line faster.

AI isn't a requirement for these projects—Super Mario 64, Ocarina of Time, and Twilight Princess were all decompiled the old-fashioned way—but it has certainly become instrumental because it's so good at this kind of reverse engineering. A lot of repos have popped up in the last few months alone that are clearly haphazard efforts by people with little experience, but those are fairly easy to recognize.

I knew AI-assisted development of these projects was an accelerator, but the pace at which the new Ocarina of Time remake hit the PC on an emulator was the moment I took serious notice. It's not a full decompilation, but the fact that someone had it running in an emulator on PC less than 24 hours after its launch was mind-blowing. This toothpaste simply isn't going back in the tube, no matter how badly Nintendo or other publishers want it to.

item.title: 4 apps that give your Google Pixel features it should've had all along
item.itunes:title: 4 apps that give your Google Pixel features it should've had all along
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Developers filling the gaps in operating systems and server platforms is nothing new. Windows users can turn to PowerToys and other open-source apps, Linux users running GNOME have Shell extensions, and Mac users have free utilities for flexible window management. Android is the same. Developers are creating apps that extend the OS's capabilities across a range of devices.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

For the Google Pixel phone in particular, there are apps worth installing that give it capabilities your phone should have had from the start. There are far too many to cover in one article, but these apps provide essential features that I wish my Pixel phone had shipped with.

Shizuku

Advanced system access for apps without root

The beauty of Android is that it's open-ish and gives users a lot of choice in what they can install. However, for some, it isn't open enough, and rooting your Pixel phone is required for advanced app functionality. That's an unnecessary step that opens the phone to potential security risks and stability issues.

Shizuku isn't a fancy app with front-facing sidebars or graphics enhancements. It provides compatible apps with access to deeper system functions that are usually out of reach. It uses Android's debugging capabilities and advanced tools without needing root access. I wish the deeper system access the app provides were an optional feature in Android.

It would be nice if it were a setting that I could toggle on my Pixel. Perhaps put it deep in advanced settings and require my password to enable it. Then I wouldn't need to take the separate step of installing it to use the complete functionality of apps like Smartspacer, Pixel IMS, and others. At least until that happens, it's available to install.

Shizuku
See at Github See at Google Play Store
I never use my Pixel phone without these powerful open-source apps

Powering my Pixel.

By  Parth Shah

Smartspacer

For a better At a Glance

The At a Glance section on my Pixel's main home screen is useful when I want to quickly see the date, weather, and other timely information like my calendar events. Android allows some customization of the space, but I would like to take it a step further. I've tried several different widgets, but it would be nice to enhance the space with native settings.

Smartspacer gives me control over what appears in the area. It supports more information sources through plugins, and I can choose when specific cards appear. I can select what data displays that's tailored to my needs. It isn't just adding another widget to the home screen. The app provides deeper control over the Pixel's existing experience. Smartspacer can work as a separate widget, but Shizuku gives it elevated access to help me customize the area.

Smartspacer
See at Github

Panels

A customizable sidebar launcher

My Pixel already provides several ways to find and switch between apps. However, it would be nice to have an easy way to open items from a sidebar-style menu while in an app. By default, it should include an easier option than going to the home screen or opening the app drawer. Something more customizable than swiping incessantly through the switcher. This is the only one with in-app purchases, but it's something I wish my Pixel had.

Depending on my workflow, I like the easy accessibility of a sidebar where I can open apps, shortcuts, or widgets. Panels is an app that provides just that. I get a sidebar that I can customize with items I frequently use, and that is easy to access with an edge swipe. It offers optional convenience and gives me access to things I use all the time. I wish it were an option to toggle on in my Pixel's settings.

Panels Sidebar Launcher
See at Google Play Store

Essentials

An open-source toolbox for Pixel

Essentials is an appropriate name for an app that adds a lot to my Pixel experience. Beyond exposing hidden settings, it lets me control familiar features. For instance, I can apply Night Light rules to individual apps instead of a general toggle. Notification edge lighting adds a visible indicator when notifications arrive. There's a Sound Mode tile to cycle between ring, vibrate, and silent. I can set up automations that trigger actions involving apps, settings, and more.

Everything included in the app isn't something my Pixel doesn't offer, but it fills many gaps by adding more. Think of it as a Good Lock for Galaxy alternative for Pixel power users. It brings several deeply hidden settings into one interface. There is a lot to play with and discover in this app that improves my all-around Pixel experience. Some permissions are available through Android Settings, but others require Shizuku for elevated access.

Essentials
See at Github

Apps that give my Pixel features it should already have

Whether from GitHub, the Play Store, or F-Droid, Android offers a lot more choice when it comes to choosing apps to install. Customization and usability are subjective, and it's all up to how you use your phone. But this handful of apps give me the options and functionality on my Pixel that I wish Google included by default. Which apps are essential on your Pixel that you wish were built-in?

I install these 5 open-source apps on every Pixel before anything else

A new Pixel is great out of the box, but these open-source apps make it even better.

What's great about this gaming monitor?

A competitive edge with 280Hz and 1440p

The 280Hz refresh rate is the main reason to look at this display. It redraws the image 280 times per second, which gives fast action in shooters and racing games a smoother look. Fast camera turns and moving targets in a shooter, or a whole scene rushing past in a racing game, are the moments where a higher refresh rate has the most to show. Pair that with a 1440p picture, and you get sharp visuals and quick motion in one screen.

When it comes to size, you have a 27-inch screen. That's enough room to keep a browser, a chat window, and a game map open side by side without everything feeling cramped, which is handy if you play and multitask on the same monitor. HDR support is listed too, so compatible games and videos can use a wider range of brightness and color. We'd treat that as a bonus rather than the main reason to buy, since we don't have a peak brightness figure for it.

Before you order, think about your PC's specs. You only see the benefit of 280Hz if your graphics card can produce enough frames to keep up, so a card that struggles in your favorite game won't get much out of it. Driving 1440p at that refresh rate also depends on the outputs and cable you connect it with, so check what your PC supports first.

It's a simple solution to the annoying problem.

Competitive players who want a 27-inch 1440p screen with a very high refresh rate are the audience here.

If you play fast-paced shooters and want a 27-inch 1440p screen with HDR and a 280Hz refresh rate, $379 at B&H after the $20 coupon is a price worth a look, especially with a gift on top. Pick up the ASUS ROG Swift Monitor if the coupon is still live when you read this.

item.title: I used a VR trick to increase my DLSS 5 frame rate, and it's what everyone should be using
item.itunes:title: I used a VR trick to increase my DLSS 5 frame rate, and it's what everyone should be using
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
DLSS 5 has quickly become one of those technologies I love using and hate benchmarking. When it works, its neural rendering can make a game look dramatically better, but the performance cost is difficult to ignore.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

I've already found ways to make that cost less painful, yet I recently stumbled across something that made me wonder if I was approaching the problem from the wrong direction entirely.

Instead of finding a way to make DLSS 5 work harder for less performance, what if I simply stopped asking it to work so hard in the first place? That's exactly what I decided to test, and the results across two very different games were not quite what I expected. In fact, I think I may have found my favorite way to run DLSS 5 yet.

Reading DLSS 5's source code finally made sense of the neural rendering complaints

DLSS 5 really does work like an AI filter, and the source code proves it

4
By  Samarveer Singh

DLSS 5 doesn't need to render every pixel equally

Foveation gives DLSS 5 a much smaller job

DLSS 5's neural rendering is impressive precisely because it does considerably more than conventional upscaling. The problem is that all that neural processing comes with a rather substantial GPU bill. Every frame gives the model an enormous amount of image data to work through, even though not every part of that frame is equally important to what I'm actually looking at.

That's where foveated rendering comes in. Instead of treating the entire image equally, it divides the frame into regions, with the highest-quality processing concentrated around a central area. After all, a tree sitting in the corner of my screen doesn't deserve the same computational budget as the character I'm staring at directly.

The further you move from the central, neurally-rendered region, the less work gets done. In fact, once you think about it, it starts sounding more and more like the most obvious optimization method.

The open-source project CheekyFoveatedDLSS takes this very VR-centric principle and applies it directly to DLSS, including neural rendering. It applies foveation to any DLSS preset, including DLSS 4.5, and now supports DLSS 5's neural rendering.

Rather than changing the game itself, it gives DLSS a different workload to chew through. Using this method, I can control how large the high-quality region is and progressively reduce the amount of the frame receiving expensive processing. So, I got curious enough to install the mod, fire up two DLSS-supported games, and find out how aggressively I could push it before I actually noticed the compromise.

Stop calling it AI slop — upscaling is democratizing high-end gaming for the 99%

Better visuals for those not on the bleeding edge.

26
By  Samarveer Singh

I put foveated DLSS 5 through its paces in The Witcher 3 Remastered

A larger fovea made neural rendering far less expensive

I started with The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt — Remastered using my DLSS 4.5 RT Ultra settings, DLSS Balanced, and three neural rendering passes enabled through a mod. I stick to three because that's where DLSS 5 earns its keep. I enabled foveation at 0.45 for both width and height.

Immediately, it looked ridiculous. The foveated region formed a rectangle in the middle of the screen, and the separation was clear as day. So, I increased both dimensions to 0.75, and I found the sweet spot — it covered my character while pushing the transition outward. So much so, that I had to look for it deliberately, and I still couldn't find the separation sometimes.

The performance difference, however, was much more interesting (and rewarding). Without foveation, using DLSS 5 dropped my baseline from 92 FPS to 56 FPS. Enabling the 0.75 preset brought that back up to 74 FPS, recovering the performance I surrendered to neural rendering.

It was really the visual behavior that made the idea click. In a game world full of foliage, the peripheral detail doesn't matter too much when DLSS 5 is making 75% of it look fantastic, and the final quarter of it is, well, unimportant. The moment I do decide to give them attention, turning the camera to bring them toward the center of the screen is enough for the fixed foveated region to cover them. Silicon alone can only do so much without software bearing the load

14
By  Samarveer Singh

Foveation isn't limited to Neural Rendering

DLSS Super Resolution can get the same treatment

CheekyFoveatedDLSS isn't actually limited to neural rendering alone. It can also apply to DLSS Super Resolution itself, which means I can reduce the work done in peripheral parts of the image before DLSS 5 even gets involved. If anything, it's another way to claw back performance without simply dropping my DLSS preset.

Super Resolution is already doing the heavy lifting of reconstructing the image from a lower internal resolution. Foveating it means the center of the screen gets the reconstruction while the edges receive less expensive treatment. Pair that with foveated Neural Rendering, and I'm telling DLSS where I want it to spend its computational budget twice.

I find that more interesting than another quality slider. Instead of choosing between "better" and "faster" globally, I can decide where quality matters and where it doesn't. For games with a strong central focus, that could make foveated DLSS a surprisingly powerful performance tool.

I gave my retro DOS games the DLSS 5 treatment, and the results were all over the place

Neural rendering in a retro gaming setup is interesting, to say the least.

1
By  Samarveer Singh

Foveated DLSS 5 might be the smartest way to run it

I'm willing to trade peripheral detail for a faster Neural Renderer

We usually talk about rendering performance as though every pixel deserves the same treatment. Foveation made me question that assumption. The center of my screen carries the information I watch, while peripheral detail is background noise.

That makes foveation different from dropping the DLSS 5 quality setting. I'm not lowering Neural Rendering quality across the image. I'm deciding where its expensive processing matters most, then letting the rest take the cheaper route.

I'm already using the new DLSS-NR model that Nvidia updated with better performance and less aggressive rendering, and now, with foveated DLSS 5, the performance cost of neural rendering is even more affordable.

That could become important as neural rendering gets more ambitious. Making the model faster will help, but making its workload smarter could be just as valuable. If three NR passes spend their time where my attention goes, every pixel doesn't need the same budget. This entire experiment changed how I think about Neural Rendering — less about making everything equally expensive, and more about making expensive work count.

I ran DLSS 5 on my PS2 games, and they finally looked like I remembered them

Nostalgia, meet neural rendering

11
By  Samarveer Singh

Maybe I've been thinking about DLSS 5 backwards

The more I play with foveated DLSS, the less convinced I am that brute-force performance is the only answer to expensive neural rendering. GPUs have never had infinite compute, and DLSS 5 certainly isn't going to change that. What can change is how intelligently we decide where that compute gets spent.

That's why I find this experiment more exciting than another performance tweak. Through this, I can give DLSS 5 fewer reasons to waste its budget. If neural rendering is going to become a bigger part of PC gaming, I suspect tricks like this will matter more and more. This is where I see the future of rendering tech going — software improving and becoming smarter instead of just another generation of GPUs throwing more silicon at the problem.

Black Friday is the best time of year to grab a quality pair of open-ear headphones, and the SHOKZ OpenRun Pro 2 is sitting at its all-time low right now. The Amazon Exclusive Rose Gold edition is down to $119.95, a full $80 off its regular $199.95 price on Amazon.

The Shokz OpenRun Pro are bone-conduction headphones that deliver open-ear audio so you can enjoy your tunes but still be aware of the world around you.

See at Amazon

Why the OpenRun Pro 2 is worth the switch

The OpenRun Pro 2 uses SHOKZ's DualPitch technology, which pairs a bone conduction driver for clear, crisp highs with a separate air conduction driver that adds deeper bass. The result is a noticeably fuller sound than you'd get from bone conduction alone, without sealing your ears off.

It's the kind of upgrade that makes you wonder why you settled for the flat, thin sound of the original. Under the hood, you get 12 hours of battery life on a single charge, which is four hours more than the previous generation. IP55 water resistance means sweat and light rain won't be an issue, and Bluetooth 5.3 keeps the connection stable even in crowded areas.

The frame is built around a nickel-titanium memory wire with an ergonomic ear hook design, so it holds its shape and stays locked in place during hard efforts. The open-ear design is the real selling point for active use.

Whether you're out on the road, on a trail, or crossing a busy intersection, you can hear traffic, pedestrians, and your surroundings while your music plays. The dual wind-resistant microphones use an AI noise reduction algorithm that filters out 96.5% of background noise on calls, and they handle wind speeds up to 15 mph.

For taking calls while you're out and about, it's a class-leading setup. But at $119.95, the Rose Gold edition is the best value in the entire lineup, and it's a color that looks genuinely distinctive rather than just another black pair of headphones. Right now, the SHOKZ OpenRun Pro 2 in Rose Gold is down $80 from its regular $199.95 price on Amazon, which is at an all-time low.

Why the OpenRun Pro 2 is worth the switch

The OpenRun Pro 2 uses SHOKZ's DualPitch technology, which pairs a bone conduction driver for clear, crisp highs with a separate air conduction driver that adds deeper bass. The result is a noticeably fuller sound than you'd get from bone conduction alone, without sealing your ears off.

It's the kind of upgrade that makes you wonder why you settled for the flat, thin sound of the original. Under the hood, you get 12 hours of battery life on a single charge, which is four hours more than the previous generation. IP55 water resistance means sweat and light rain won't be an issue, and Bluetooth 5.3 keeps the connection stable even in crowded areas.

The frame is built around a nickel-titanium memory wire with an ergonomic ear hook design, so it holds its shape and stays locked in place during hard efforts. The open-ear design is the real selling point for active use.

Whether you're out on the road, on a trail, or crossing a busy intersection, you can hear traffic, pedestrians, and your surroundings while your music plays. The dual wind-resistant microphones use an AI noise reduction algorithm that filters out 96.5% of background noise on calls, and they handle wind speeds up to 15 mph.

For taking calls while you're out and about, it's a class-leading setup. But at $119.95, the Rose Gold edition is the best value in the entire lineup, and it's a color that looks genuinely distinctive rather than just another black pair of headphones.
